Comparative Advantage

The one true, non-obvious idea

True, non-trivial, two centuries old, and still argued against by people who understand it.

2 min read3 figures, each sourcedWhere it is contestedUpdated 19 September 2026
On this pageBy the numbersHow it happenedWho did the workWhere it is contestedWhat I changed my mind aboutGo to the sourceReads across to

Asked to name one proposition in the social sciences that is both true and non-trivial, Samuelson named this one — and noted how long it takes people to believe it.

If you keep one line

Your absolute skill is irrelevant. The ratio of what you give up is everything.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Ricardo's 1817 example is England and Portugal, cloth and wine. Portugal can produce both more cheaply in absolute terms. Trade still benefits both, because what each gives up to produce a unit of one good — the opportunity cost — differs. The better producer of everything should still specialise where its edge is largest and buy the rest. The result is counterintuitive enough that people who understand it perfectly still argue against it in practice, because it is stated in relative terms and human intuition runs on absolutes.

It scales down, which is why it's on this shelf rather than in a textbook. It's the argument for why a founder who is the best engineer in the building should not be writing the code, and why the fastest person on a team should hand off work they would genuinely do better themselves. Absolute skill is irrelevant. The ratio of what you give up is everything, and almost every overloaded competent person is violating this right now.

The honest caveats are large and usually omitted by people quoting Samuelson. The theorem says gains are available in aggregate, not that they're distributed. Ricardo assumed capital stayed home, which it conspicuously does not. And the compensation the welfare argument quietly assumes — winners pay losers — is politically optional and mostly hasn't happened.

Autor, Dorn and Hanson measured where the losses landed. Chinese import competition is associated with roughly 985,000 lost US manufacturing jobs between 1999 and 2011, and around 2.4 million across all sectors once you include supply chains and local demand effects — concentrated in specific commuting zones where wages and participation stayed depressed for at least a decade. Both things are true: the aggregate gains were real, and so were the concentrated, persistent, geographically specific losses.

01By the numbers

1817On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, John Murray: David Ricardo (Econlib edition)
985,000US manufacturing jobs lost to the China shock, 1999–2011 (≈2.4M across all sectors): David Autor, David Dorn & Gordon Hanson, 'The China Shock', Annual Review of Economics 8, 2016
10 yrs+How long affected local labour markets stayed depressed: Autor, Dorn & Hanson, 'The China Shock', Annual Review of Economics 8, 2016

02How it happened

  1. 1776Adam Smith makes the case for specialisation, but on absolute advantage.
  2. 1817Ricardo's 'Principles' states comparative advantage; the wine-and-cloth example is barely two pages.
  3. 1940sStolper and Samuelson show who inside a country wins and loses — the distributional footnote that became the main event.
  4. 1969Samuelson answers Ulam's challenge: comparative advantage is the true, non-trivial proposition.
  5. 2013Autor, Dorn and Hanson measure the China shock's local labour-market effects.
  6. 2016–The distributional finding, not the theorem, drives a decade of trade politics.

03Who did the work

David RicardoA stockbroker who retired rich and then wrote the argument economists have been re-explaining ever since.
Paul SamuelsonNamed it as economics' one true non-obvious result, and wrote about why nobody believes it.
David AutorMeasured what the theorem's aggregate framing leaves out, and changed the politics of trade doing it.

04Where it is contested

The theorem is not in dispute; its policy sufficiency is. Ricardo assumed immobile capital, adjustment is neither costless nor fast, and 'trade is good on net' and 'this trade policy is good' are separate claims that get deliberately conflated in both directions.

05What I changed my mind about

I used to deploy this as a conversation-ending fact and treat objectors as innumerate. The China shock literature is the reason I stopped. The theorem is still true; my use of it was sloppy, because I was answering a distributional question with an aggregate result and calling the other person confused.
